newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan rebels face tough political future.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan rebels face tough political future.

text.p: Despite an agreement signed in Madrid allowing Guatemala's leftist rebels to return legally to normal life, the guerrillas face a tough political future, analysts said on Thursday.

"They lost the military war ... and they are entering (political life) under the condition that they not be an obstacle for the army or big business," Hector Rosada, a former government peace negotiator, told Reuters.

The Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG), formed in 1981 to unite four separate guerrilla fronts, plans to form a political party after a definitive peace treaty is signed on Dec. 29, ending 36 years of civil war.

"Within one or two years we will have fully organised the party and we will be prepared and ready to participate in the next elections," guerrilla commander Pablo Monsanto told reporters this week in Madrid.

Rosada said the URNG could take a fair share of votes but has lost support in the last year after compromising much of its ideology during peace negotiations. "During this year, they have completely betrayed their position as the people's vanguard. They have signed a series of accords that, far from coinciding with the demands of the grass roots, damages them."

Retired Gen. Hector Alejandro Gramajo, a former defence minister, said the URNG might be able to win 6 percent to 10 percent of the vote in an election. But he said it had lost credibility since October, when a guerrilla was arrested on charges of kidnapping an elderly woman from a leading family and holding her for a multimillion-dollar ransom.

Gramajo and others agree the kidnapping lost the URNG its best candidate when Rodrigo Asturias, also known as Comandante Gaspar Ilom, was forced from his position at the peace talks because of a possible connection with the abduction.

"Imagine a ticket with Ilom and (1992 Nobel Peace Prize winner) Rigoberta Menchu. That would have been formidable," Amilcar Mendez, one of four members of congress from the leftist New Guatemala Democratic Front (FDNG), said.

The URNG has said it wants to unite with other leftist parties to form a progressive block in Congress, but Guatemala's left is not exactly opening its arms. Mendez said the FDNG had not committed itself to more than cooperating with the URNG in a nation-building project down the road.
"The unification of the left will not be possible. There are too many self-destructive elements," Rosada said.
Historically, the URNG itself has had more internal divisions than other Central American guerrilla forces, less international support and less grass-roots support.

Nicaraguan Sandinistas won a civil war and formed a strong political force that still exists, although it no longer holds power. In El Salvador, guerrillas controlled large regions of the country and were able to threaten the capital when they entered into peace negotiations with the government.

The URNG was strongest in 1981, before the scorched-earth counterinsurgency campaign by the army orchestrated by the military governments of Gen. Romeo Lucas Garcia and Gen. Efrain Rios Montt. By 1984, after four years of massacres and political assassinations had terrorised potential URNG supporters, the army had won the military battle.
The government began to negotiate a peace with the guerrillas in 1991 because of international pressure to demilitarize Guatemalan politics, Rosada said.

Until now membership in the URNG had been illegal and rebels lived clandestinely in fighting units in the mountains or in exile in Mexico, El Salvador and elsewhere. Early next year the guerrillas -- 3,000 of them, according to the URNG; fewer than 1,000, according to the army -- will gather in camps and turn in their arms under international scrutiny.

Under the accord signed on Thursday in Madrid, guerrillas will be free to live openly in Guatemala. The accord gives them amnesty for political crimes against the state, sedition, rebellion and illegal possession of arms.
